hints: Think of OILRIG for electrons and ask yourself what happens to Na when it forms $\text{Na}^{+}$ in $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Link reducing agent to electrons**
Picture Na atoms turning into $\text{Na}^{+}$ ions. Each Na loses one electron, $\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+} + e^{-}$. Losing electrons is oxidation, and the species that is oxidised causes the other reactant to be reduced. That is exactly what a reducing agent does, it donates electrons to the other species.
Final answer: A species that donates electrons.

hints: Recall the general behaviour of a Group 1 metal oxide with water and what type of solution it forms.
walkthrough:
Predict the product**
$\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$ is a strongly basic oxide. Basic oxides react with water to give the metal hydroxide, so you expect sodium hydroxide, $\text{NaOH}$, only. Balance Na and H by using 2 $\text{NaOH}$: $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$.

hints: Think of the prefix amphi meaning both, and recall what $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ does with $\text{HCl}$ and with $\text{NaOH}$.
walkthrough:
Unpack the word amphoteric**
Amphoteric simply means can act two ways. $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ reacts with acids to form Al salts like $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, showing basic behaviour, and also reacts with bases like $\text{NaOH}$ to form aluminates, showing acidic behaviour.
Final answer: Reacts with both acids and bases / shows both acidic and basic behaviour.

hints: Remember the colourless aluminate product is $\text{NaAl(OH)}_{4}$ and that water is also a reactant alongside $\text{NaOH}$.
walkthrough:
Build the equation**
This is the acidic side of $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ reacting with a base. The product given by the purification is the soluble complex $\text{NaAl(OH)}_{4}$. To balance Al you need 2 of these, which then needs 2 $\text{NaOH}$ and 3 $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to balance Na, O and H: $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl(OH)}_{4}$.

hints: Recall what a catalyst does to the reaction pathway and how this is shown as a new activation energy line on a Boltzmann curve.
Think about how lowering $E_{A}$ changes the area under the curve to the right of $E_{A}$.
Link the larger fraction of molecules able to react to the rate in terms of collisions.
walkthrough:
Show the lower activation energy**
A catalyst never changes the starting molecules or the Boltzmann curve itself. It gives a new route with a lower hump to climb. On Fig. 2.1 you would mark the original $E_{A}$ to the right and the catalysed $E_{A,cat}$ to the left of it.

Read the area under the curve**
Only molecules with energy at or beyond the $E_{A}$ line can react on collision. Moving that line left means a much larger area under the curve lies beyond it. So a greater proportion of molecules now have $E \geqslant E_{A}$.

Convert to collisions and rate**
More molecules able to react means many more collisions per second result in reaction. The frequency of effective collisions increases, so the dehydration is faster at the same temperature.

Final answer: Catalyst provides an alternative route of lower activation energy, $E_{A,cat} < E_{A}$.
A greater proportion of molecules have $E \geqslant E_{A}$.
Frequency of effective collisions increases so rate increases.

hints: Use the melting point of $24^{\circ}\text{C}$ to decide between giant lattice and small separate molecules.
Use the fact that it reacts with water to form an acid to decide between ionic and covalent bonding for a Period 3 oxide.
walkthrough:
Deduce structure from melting point**
$24^{\circ}\text{C}$ is very low, it melts just above room temperature. A giant ionic or giant covalent lattice would need huge energy to break strong lattice bonds and would melt at hundreds or thousands of degrees. This must be separate $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{6}$ molecules held by weak London forces, so simple molecular.

Deduce bonding from reaction with water**
Ionic oxides tend to give simple hydroxide solutions, while covalent molecular oxides are hydrolysed to give acids. Here $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{6}$ reacts to give $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{3}$, an acid, which points to covalent P-O bonds being broken by water.

Final answer: Structure is simple / molecular because it has a low melting point.
Bonding is covalent because it is hydrolysed / reacts with water.

hints: Set the sum $3(+1) + P + 3(-2) = 0$ using the usual $+1$ for H and $-2$ for O.
walkthrough:
Apply the oxidation number rules**
In $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{3}$, H is $+1$ and O is $-2$. Let P be $x$: $$3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0$$ $$3 + x - 6 = 0$$ $$x = +3$$
Final answer: +3 / III

hints: Write $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{f}(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_{f}(\text{reactants})$ for $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{6}(\text{s}) + 2\text{O}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}(\text{s})$ and remember $\Delta H_{f}(\text{O}_{2}) = 0$.
walkthrough:
Solve using the formation cycle**
For the reaction: $$\Delta H_{r} = \Delta H_{f}(\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}) - [\Delta H_{f}(\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{6}) + 2\Delta H_{f}(\text{O}_{2})]$$ $\text{O}_{2}$ in its standard state is zero, so: $$-1372 = -3012 - \Delta H_{f}(\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{6})$$ Rearranging: $$\Delta H_{f}(\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{6}) = -3012 + 1372 = -1640 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Final answer: $-1640$ ($\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$)

hints: Recall that $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ is the full anhydride of phosphoric acid $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ and balance water to supply H and O.
walkthrough:
Form the acid**
$\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ is strongly acidic and fully hydrolysed to $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$. With 4 P on the left you need 4 acids on the right, which needs 12 H and therefore 6 $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$: $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$.

hints: Think about what must happen to NO from equation 1 to reform $\text{NO}_{2}$, and which atmospheric gas provides the oxygen.
walkthrough:
Close the catalytic loop**
In equation 1, $\text{NO}_{2}$ is used up and NO is made. For $\text{NO}_{2}$ to be a catalyst it must be remade. NO is reoxidised by atmospheric oxygen: $\text{NO} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow \text{NO}_{2}$. Adding the two steps gives the overall $\text{SO}_{2} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow \text{SO}_{3}$.

hints: Recall the well known eye irritant formed from $\text{NO}_{2}$ and unburned hydrocarbons in sunlight.
walkthrough:
Name the smog component**
Sunlight driven reactions of $\text{NO}_{2}$ with unburned hydrocarbons produce a mixture including ozone, aldehydes and the key pollutant peroxyacetylnitrate, shortened to PAN.
Final answer: peroxyacetylnitrate / PAN

hints: Read the temperatures at 20 km and 50 km from Fig. 2.2 and decide which height is colder.
Apply Le Chatelier to equation 1 with $\Delta H_{r} = -168 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to predict the shift when temperature falls.
walkthrough:
Compare the temperatures**
Look at Fig. 2.2. At about 20 km the temperature is near $-55^{\circ}\text{C}$, while at about 50 km it is near $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. So 20 km is significantly colder than 50 km.

Apply Le Chatelier**
Equation 1 has $\Delta H_{r} = -168 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, so the forward direction $\text{SO}_{2} + \text{NO}_{2} \rightleftharpoons \text{SO}_{3} + \text{NO}$ is exothermic. Lowering the temperature favours the exothermic side to release heat, so equilibrium shifts further to the right at the colder 20 km height.

Final answer: Position of equilibrium moves / further to right at 20 km.
Forward reaction is exothermic and temperature is colder at 20 km (cf. 50 km).
